pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Define abstraction, data/state/operation separation, contracts, preconditions and postconditions; distinguish an ADT from one implementation.

### Invariant / contract
ADT operations describe what is allowed without committing to storage.

### Complexity
Depends on interface choices rather than physical layout; common operations are insert, delete, access, search, size and iteration.

### Why it matters
A list interface can be implemented using an array or linked nodes without changing client-level meaning.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Define abstraction, data/state/operation separation, contracts, preconditions and postconditions; distinguish an ADT from one implementation.

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Abstract Data Types (ADTs) and List ADT**?
options: ADT operations describe what is allowed without committing to storage.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Abstract Data Types (ADTs) and List ADT is: ADT operations describe what is allowed without committing to storage.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Implement a list with a contiguous array, maintain logical size separately from capacity, and reason about shifting and resizing.

### Invariant / contract
Elements in positions [0,size) are valid logical elements; unused capacity lies outside that range.

### Complexity
Access O(1); middle insertion/deletion O(n); append amortized O(1) in a dynamic array.

### Why it matters
Dynamic arrays are useful when indexed access and cache-friendly traversal matter.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Implement a list with a contiguous array, maintain logical size separately from capacity, and reason about shifting and resizing.

The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Array-Based List Implementation is: Elements in positions [0,size) are valid logical elements; unused capacity lies outside that range.

Build nodes and links, maintain head/tail metadata, and understand pointer-based storage and traversal.

### Invariant / contract
Every reachable node is linked exactly once from the head in a well-formed singly list.

### Complexity
Traversal O(n), head insertion O(1), tail insertion O(1) when tail is maintained.

### Why it matters
Linked storage trades direct indexing for flexible local updates.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Insert and remove nodes at the front, end, and arbitrary positions while preserving links.

### Invariant / contract
Before reconnecting links, preserve any node that would otherwise become unreachable.

### Complexity
Known-node updates can be O(1); finding the position/value is typically O(n).

### Why it matters
Dummy/sentinel nodes can simplify boundary cases.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Insert and remove nodes at the front, end, and arbitrary positions while preserving links.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Model lists whose last node points back to the first; implement insertion, deletion, and bounded traversal.

### Invariant / contract
A non-empty circular list satisfies tail.next == head and has no null terminator.

### Complexity
With a tail pointer, front and back insertion can be O(1).

### Why it matters
Useful for cyclic scheduling and round-robin processing.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Model lists whose last node points back to the first; implement insertion, deletion, and bounded traversal.

checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Circular Linked Lists is: A non-empty circular list satisfies tail.next == head and has no null terminator.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`linked state 10 → 20 → 30, with head/tail (and prev where applicable) marked before and after the operation.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Infinite traversal loops, singleton deletion, head/tail synchronization.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Maintain prev/next links, support forward and backward traversal, and perform O(1) unlinking when a node is known.

### Invariant / contract
For every adjacent pair, a.next.prev == a and b.prev.next == b.

### Complexity
Known-node insertion/deletion O(1), search O(n), extra pointer per node.

### Why it matters
Doubly linked lists are a common building block for LRU caches and undo/redo.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Maintain prev/next links, support forward and backward traversal, and perform O(1) unlinking when a node is known.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Compare array-based and linked representations, sentinel nodes, two-pointer techniques, and common interview transformations.

### Invariant / contract
The chosen representation must preserve the required API and complexity promises.

### Complexity
Representation determines access/update costs; pattern choice determines interview complexity.

### Why it matters
This topic bridges classroom ADTs and interview-style linked-list problem solving.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Compare array-based and linked representations, sentinel nodes, two-pointer techniques, and common interview transformations.

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**?
options: The chosen representation must preserve the required API and complexity promises.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns is: The chosen representation must preserve the required API and complexity promises.

pages.title: Pattern Recognition
pages.content:
### When should you think about **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

options: The problem title contains the word “data”.
The required operation and constraints match the structure’s strengths and invariant.
The input is large, so any data structure will automatically be optimal.
A solution is correct only when it uses recursion.
checkpoint.explanation: Pattern recognition comes from the operation/query requirements and constraints, not from keywords alone.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`linked state 10 → 20 → 30, with head/tail (and prev where applicable) marked before and after the operation.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<int>a={1,2,3};reverse(a.begin(),a.end());for(int x:a)cout<<x<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Only the final printed value.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
The chosen representation must preserve the required API and complexity promises.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Overengineering, unnecessary extra passes, ignoring constraints.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns.

codeCard.code:

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**?
options: Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

pages.title: Micro Practice
pages.content:
Try a tiny variation before opening a full solution. Change exactly one thing in the previous example: the empty case, a single element, a duplicate key, a boundary index, or one additional edge/node.

### Micro-practice
For **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**, change one condition from the dry run—such as an empty structure, a boundary position, a duplicate key, a disconnected vertex, a repeated value, or a different constraint. Predict the new state first, then implement only the changed step.

**Checkpoint:** state the invariant before running and state what changed after running.

callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns.

checkpoint.question: What should a micro-practice attempt for **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns** change first?

One controlled boundary or state variation while keeping the core invariant unchanged.
The complexity requirement without changing the algorithm.
The problem statement and output contract.

pages.content:
Now solve the topic’s skill-builder and the mapped interview problems without copying the implementation. Start with the easiest problem, write the brute-force idea, then derive the List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns solution.

**Before submit:** record the expected complexity, list three edge cases, and state one correctness invariant.

checkpoint.question: Before submitting an independent problem on **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**, which combination is most important?

Only the fastest-looking code, without proving correctness.
Only the number of lines of code.
Only the sample output.
checkpoint.explanation: Production-quality DSA practice combines correctness reasoning, edge-case coverage, and complexity analysis.

pages.title: Mastery Gate
pages.content:
### Mastery checklist for **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**
- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.
- Identify when the pattern applies.
- Dry-run a fresh example.
- Implement the core operation without scaffolding.
- State correctness/invariant reasoning.
- State time and space complexity.
- Identify at least three edge cases.
- Solve one LeetCode transfer problem relevant to this topic.

**Common failure to avoid:** Overengineering, unnecessary extra passes, ignoring constraints.

checkpoint.question: Which outcome demonstrates mastery of **List Design Trade-offs and Interview Patterns**?
options: Explain the pattern, implement it on an unseen case, justify correctness/complexity, and transfer it to interview practice.
Copy a memorized solution without tracing it.
Solve only the exact example seen in the lesson.
Recall the definition but cannot implement it.
checkpoint.explanation: Mastery requires explanation, implementation, reasoning, and transfer—not recall alone.

questions.question: What does an ADT specify?
options: The observable operations and behavioral contract independent of one implementation.
A single pointer representation.
A fixed memory layout.
Only the syntax of one language.
questions.explanation: The observable operations and behavioral contract independent of one implementation.

questions.question: Why is array-based middle insertion typically O(n)?
options: Because indexed access becomes O(log n).
Because the array must be converted to a linked list.
Elements after the insertion point may need to shift right.
Because arrays cannot store duplicates.
questions.explanation: Elements after the insertion point may need to shift right.

questions.question: Which invariant describes logical size in an array-based list?
options: The physical array length always equals logical size.
The list must remain sorted.
Valid logical elements occupy the range from index 0 through size-1.
Every capacity slot must contain a valid element.
questions.explanation: Valid logical elements occupy the range from index 0 through size-1.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of maintaining a tail pointer in a singly linked list?
options: It makes searching O(1).
It makes indexed access O(1).
It can make insertion at the end O(1).
It eliminates the need for a head pointer.
questions.explanation: It can make insertion at the end O(1).

questions.question: Which pointer is essential for iterative list reversal?
options: A queue containing all node values.
A sorted copy of every node.
A second head that is never updated.
A saved next pointer prevents the remaining list from being lost.
questions.explanation: A saved next pointer prevents the remaining list from being lost.

questions.question: When deleting the head of a singly linked list, what must happen?
options: Always move tail to the previous node.
Sort all remaining nodes.
Move head to the next node and handle the empty-list case.
Change the data value of every node.
questions.explanation: Move head to the next node and handle the empty-list case.

questions.question: What must always be true in a non-empty circular singly linked list with a tail pointer?
options: head.prev points to tail.
tail.next points to head.
Every node has two outgoing links.
tail.next is null.
questions.explanation: tail.next points to head.

questions.question: Why is a doubly linked list useful for LRU-style recency operations?
options: It automatically sorts nodes.
A known node can be unlinked and moved in O(1) pointer updates.
It provides O(1) search by value.
It removes the need for a hash map.
questions.explanation: A known node can be unlinked and moved in O(1) pointer updates.

questions.question: What is the main risk when deleting a node while traversing with an iterator/pointer?
options: The data type of remaining nodes changes.
The traversal position can become invalid or skip a node.
The list automatically becomes sorted.
Every deletion becomes O(1) regardless of search cost.
questions.explanation: The traversal position can become invalid or skip a node.

questions.question: Which application naturally benefits from a doubly linked list?
options: Undo/redo or an LRU cache.
Direct matrix multiplication.
Hash computation alone.
Binary search on a sorted array.
questions.explanation: Undo/redo or an LRU cache.

questions.question: What does a sentinel/dummy node mainly improve?
options: It removes all memory overhead.
It guarantees O(1) search.
It sorts the list automatically.
It reduces special-case branching around list boundaries.
questions.explanation: It reduces special-case branching around list boundaries.

questions.question: Which operation is genuinely O(1) on a singly linked list when the target node reference is already known and deletion uses a suitable predecessor model?
options: A local link update.
Searching for an arbitrary value.
Computing the sorted order of all values.
Finding the kth node from the head.
questions.explanation: A local link update.

questions.question: Why can linked lists be slower than arrays even for O(n) traversal?
options: Pointer chasing can reduce locality and increase indirection.
Arrays cannot be traversed sequentially.
Linked lists always use O(n^2) time.
Linked lists require hashing every element.
questions.explanation: Pointer chasing can reduce locality and increase indirection.

questions.question: Which representation is best suited to frequent random indexed access?
options: A singly linked list.
An array-based list.
A node chain accessed by repeated next pointers.
A circular list without indexing metadata.
questions.explanation: An array-based list.

questions.question: What must a robust list API define for deletion of a missing value?
options: A requirement to sort before every deletion.
A requirement to corrupt the list.
The behavioral outcome for a target that is not present.
A requirement to resize even for linked storage.
questions.explanation: The behavioral outcome for a target that is not present.

questions.question: Which technique is commonly used to find the middle of a linked list in one pass?
options: Two nested loops over array indices.
Binary search.
Fast and slow pointers.
Heapify.
questions.explanation: Fast and slow pointers.

questions.question: Which statement about list ADT and implementation is correct?
options: Only arrays can implement a list.
Multiple implementations can satisfy the same ADT contract.
An ADT and a class must have identical fields.
Only linked nodes can implement a list.
questions.explanation: Multiple implementations can satisfy the same ADT contract.

questions.question: What is the main cost of a doubly linked list compared with a singly linked list?
options: An extra pointer per node and more pointer updates.
Mandatory sorting after insertion.
Loss of backward traversal.
O(log n) search instead of O(n).
questions.explanation: An extra pointer per node and more pointer updates.

questions.question: Which property must be checked after every pointer mutation?
options: That the list height stays logarithmic.
The structure still satisfies its link and boundary invariants.
That all nodes are contiguous in memory.
That all values are unique.
questions.explanation: The structure still satisfies its link and boundary invariants.

questions.question: Which interview progression is most appropriate after basic singly linked-list operations?
options: B-tree deletion → hashing only.
Heapify → matrix multiplication.
Reverse → two pointers → cycle/intersection → advanced rearrangement.
Sorting arrays only → recursion only.
questions.explanation: Reverse → two pointers → cycle/intersection → advanced rearrangement.

learningObjectives: Define ADTs and separate a list contract from its physical representation.
Implement and analyze array-based lists including logical size, capacity, shifting, and resizing.
Implement singly, circular, and doubly linked lists with correct head/tail/prev/next invariants.
Use iterator-safe traversal and mutation while handling empty, singleton, and boundary cases.
Choose array versus linked representations from operation frequency, locality, and complexity requirements.
Apply list patterns such as reversal, fast/slow pointers, merging, rotation, and recency ordering.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Define LIFO behavior, push/pop/top semantics, error states, and complexity contracts.

### Invariant / contract
The most recently inserted active element is the only removable element.

### Complexity
Push/pop/top should be O(1) with a suitable implementation.

### Why it matters
Stacks model nesting, backtracking, and call frames.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Define LIFO behavior, push/pop/top semantics, error states, and complexity contracts.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){vector<int>s; s.push_back(10);s.push_back(20);cout<<s.back()<<" ";s.pop_back();cout<<s.back();}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Stack ADT and Operations**?
options: The most recently inserted active element is the only removable element.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Stack ADT and Operations is: The most recently inserted active element is the only removable element.

pages.title: Pattern Recognition
pages.content:
### When should you think about **Stack ADT and Operations**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`stack bottom→top [10, 20, 30] and process the next token/operation from the top.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Stack ADT and Operations.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){stack<int>s;for(int x:{3,1,4})s.push(x);cout<<s.top();}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Stack ADT and Operations**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Only the final printed value.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
The most recently inserted active element is the only removable element.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Underflow, wrong end of structure.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Stack ADT and Operations.

codeCard.code:

using namespace std;int main(){stack<int>s;for(int x:{3,1,4})s.push(x);cout<<s.top();}

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Stack ADT and Operations**?
options: Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

pages.content:
Try a tiny variation before opening a full solution. Change exactly one thing in the previous example: the empty case, a single element, a duplicate key, a boundary index, or one additional edge/node.

pages.content:
### Mastery checklist for **Stack ADT and Operations**
- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.
- Identify when the pattern applies.

- Implement the core operation without scaffolding.
- State correctness/invariant reasoning.

- Identify at least three edge cases.

- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.
- Identify when the pattern applies.
- Dry-run a fresh example.
- Implement the core operation without scaffolding.
- State correctness/invariant reasoning.
- State time and space complexity.
- Identify at least three edge cases.
- Solve one LeetCode transfer problem relevant to this topic.

**Common failure to avoid:** Mixing stack state with unrelated counters.

callout.title: Mastery takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Applications of Stacks — Parsing and Backtracking.

checkpoint.question: Which outcome demonstrates mastery of **Applications of Stacks — Parsing and Backtracking**?
options: Explain the pattern, implement it on an unseen case, justify correctness/complexity, and transfer it to interview practice.
Solve only the exact example seen in the lesson.
Copy a memorized solution without tracing it.
Recall the definition but cannot implement it.
checkpoint.explanation: Mastery requires explanation, implementation, reasoning, and transfer—not recall alone.

codeExamples.label: C++
codeExamples.title: Applications of Stacks — Parsing and Backtracking — concept example
codeExamples.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){string s="a(b(c)d)e";vector<int>st;for(int i=0;i<(int)s.size();++i){if(s[i]=='(')st.push_back(i);else if(s[i]==')'){cout<<i-st.back()<<" ";st.pop_back();}}}

codeExamples.label: C++
codeExamples.title: Applications of Stacks — Parsing and Backtracking — implementation/pattern example
codeExamples.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<int>choices={1,2,3};vector<int>st,cur;for(int x:choices){st.push_back(x);cur.push_back(x);}while(!cur.empty()){cout<<cur.back()<<" ";cur.pop_back();st.pop_back();}}

topics.learningTrack: Prerequisite → Concept → Recognition → Dry Run → Guided Build → Micro Practice → Independent Practice → LeetCode Transfer → Mastery

steps.title: Check prerequisites
steps.goal: Stack operations.
steps.action: Recall the prerequisite and pass the tiny self-check before continuing.
steps.exitCriteria: I can explain the prerequisite without opening another lesson.

steps.title: Build the mental model
steps.goal: Use stacks for undo, depth-first state, delimiter matching, and nested structures.
steps.action: Read the rule, identify the representation, and state the invariant in your own words.
steps.exitCriteria: I can describe what the structure stores/changes and why it exists.

steps.title: Learn when to use it
steps.goal: Recognize Applications of Stacks — Parsing and Backtracking from operation patterns and constraints.
steps.action: Classify two small scenarios and explain why the topic does or does not fit.
steps.exitCriteria: I can give at least two recognition signals and one non-fit condition.

steps.title: Trace a tiny example
steps.goal: Track every pointer, index, stack/queue position, tree relation, graph state, or hash-table slot involved.
steps.action: Simulate the algorithm on paper and re-check the invariant after each transition.
steps.exitCriteria: I can predict the final state/output for a fresh small case.

steps.title: Guided implementation
steps.goal: Translate the invariant into small code steps and handle boundary cases deliberately.
steps.action: Write the state variables first, then implement one invariant-preserving transition at a time.
steps.exitCriteria: The implementation works on the base case and at least one boundary case.

steps.title: Micro practice
steps.goal: Transfer the rule to one controlled variation.
steps.action: Change exactly one boundary or state condition and predict the effect before running code.
steps.exitCriteria: I can repair one small variation without copying the original solution.

steps.title: Independent practice
steps.goal: Solve the skill builder and increasing-difficulty practice.
steps.action: State baseline, pattern, invariant, complexity, and edge cases before coding.
steps.exitCriteria: I can submit an unseen problem without scaffolding.

steps.title: Mastery gate
steps.goal: Explain and transfer the topic to interview-style practice.
steps.action: Complete the topic checklist and at least one mapped LeetCode problem when available.
steps.exitCriteria: I can explain, implement, analyze, and transfer the technique.

problemSolvingChecklist: What exactly is the input and output?
Which operation/relationship dominates the problem?
What invariant must remain true?
What is the baseline solution?
What repeated work can be removed?
Which data structure best supports the required operations?
What edge cases challenge the representation?
What are the time and auxiliary-space costs?

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Convert infix expressions using precedence and associativity rules, then evaluate the resulting postfix form.

### Invariant / contract
The operator stack holds operators not yet emitted whose precedence has not been resolved.

### Complexity
O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space.

### Why it matters
The shunting-yard idea separates parsing from evaluation.

callout.text: Convert infix expressions using precedence and associativity rules, then evaluate the resulting postfix form.

### Guided dry run

1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

codeExamples.label: C++
codeExamples.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion — concept example
codeExamples.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){string s="a+b*c";vector<char>op;string out;auto prec=[](char c){return c=='+'||c=='-'?1:c=='*'||c=='/'?2:3;};for(char c:s){if(isalnum(c))out+=c;else if(c=='(')op.push_back(c);else if(c==')'){while(op.back()!='('){out+=op.back();op.pop_back();}op.pop_back();}else{while(!op.empty()&&op.back()!='('&&prec(op.back())>=prec(c)){out+=op.back();op.pop_back();}op.push_back(c);}}while(!op.empty()){out+=op.back();op.pop_back();}cout<<out;}

codeExamples.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion — implementation/pattern example

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){string s="a^b^c";vector<char>op;string out;for(char c:s){if(isalpha(c))out+=c;else{while(!op.empty()&&op.back()!='('&&(op.back()!='^'||c!='^')){out+=op.back();op.pop_back();}op.push_back(c);}}while(!op.empty()){out+=op.back();op.pop_back();}cout<<out;}

### Core idea
Relate function activation records to stacks and trace recursive execution/return order.

### Invariant / contract
Each active call owns parameters, locals, and a return position until it completes.

### Complexity
Depth O(h) for recursion; work depends on recurrence.

### Why it matters
Understanding call-stack state makes recursion less mysterious.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Implement fixed-capacity circular buffers using modular arithmetic and distinguish full from empty states.

### Invariant / contract
front points to the first live item; rear points to the next insertion slot under the chosen convention.

### Complexity
O(1) enqueue/dequeue; O(capacity) space.

### Why it matters
A circular array reuses freed slots without shifting elements.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Implement fixed-capacity circular buffers using modular arithmetic and distinguish full from empty states.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){int a[4]={0};int front=0,rear=0,cap=4; a[rear]=10;rear=(rear+1)%cap;a[rear]=20;rear=(rear+1)%cap;cout<<a[front]<<" ";front=(front+1)%cap;cout<<a[front];}

Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Circular Queue is: front points to the first live item; rear points to the next insertion slot under the chosen convention.

pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`queue/deque state front→back [10, 20, 30], then trace one enqueue/dequeue or two-ended update.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

options: front points to the first live item; rear points to the next insertion slot under the chosen convention.

codeExamples.label: C++
codeExamples.title: Circular Queue — concept example
codeExamples.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;class CQ{vector<int>a;int f=0,r=0,c=0;public:CQ(int n):a(n){}bool enq(int x){if(c==(int)a.size())return false;a[r]=x;r=(r+1)%a.size();++c;return true;}bool deq(){if(!c)return false;f=(f+1)%a.size();--c;return true;}int front()const{return a[f];}};int main(){CQ q(3);q.enq(1);q.enq(2);q.deq();q.enq(3);q.enq(4);cout<<q.front();}

codeExamples.title: Circular Queue — implementation/pattern example

using namespace std;int main(){int a[5]={0},f=0,r=0,n=5;for(int x:{7,8,9}){a[r]=x;r=(r+1)%n;}cout<<a[f]<<" ";f=(f+1)%n;a[r]=10;r=(r+1)%n;cout<<a[f]<<" "<<a[(r+n-1)%n];}

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`queue/deque state front→back [10, 20, 30], then trace one enqueue/dequeue or two-ended update.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

questions.question: What does LIFO mean for a stack?
options: The smallest item is removed first.
The most recently inserted active item is removed first.
The oldest item is removed first.
Items are removed in sorted order.
questions.explanation: The most recently inserted active item is removed first.

questions.question: Which stack operation should normally be O(1)?
options: Search by arbitrary value in an array stack.
Sorting the entire stack.
push, pop, and top.
Finding the minimum without augmentation.
questions.explanation: push, pop, and top.

questions.question: Which invariant is useful for balanced-symbol checking?
options: The stack contains exactly the unmatched opening symbols for the processed prefix.
The stack contains every character seen so far.
The stack is always sorted alphabetically.
The stack contains only closing symbols.
questions.explanation: The stack contains exactly the unmatched opening symbols for the processed prefix.

questions.question: In postfix evaluation, why are two operands popped for a binary operator?
options: Because every operator is unary.
Because the queue front is needed.
The operator combines the two most recent operand values in reverse stack order.
Because postfix requires sorting first.
questions.explanation: The operator combines the two most recent operand values in reverse stack order.

questions.question: Why is infix-to-postfix conversion useful?
options: It guarantees every expression is recursive.
It separates precedence handling from later stack-based evaluation.
It turns every operator into a queue operation.
It removes the need to parse operators.
questions.explanation: It separates precedence handling from later stack-based evaluation.

questions.question: What causes recursion to consume call-stack space?
options: Each active call keeps its local state and return context until it returns.
The compiler creates a new heap for each call.
Each call sorts all previous frames.
Recursion always allocates an entire array.
questions.explanation: Each active call keeps its local state and return context until it returns.

questions.question: What does FIFO mean for a queue?
options: The highest priority item is removed first.
The smallest numeric item is removed first.
The earliest active item is removed first.
The newest item is removed first.
questions.explanation: The earliest active item is removed first.

questions.question: Why is a circular queue better than shifting an array after every dequeue?
options: It makes random access O(log n).
It removes the need for capacity tracking.
It sorts the queue automatically.
Freed slots are reused with modular index movement.
questions.explanation: Freed slots are reused with modular index movement.

questions.question: What is the usual purpose of a deque?
options: Support efficient insertion/removal at both ends.
Support only middle insertion.
Guarantee sorted order.
Replace every tree traversal.
questions.explanation: Support efficient insertion/removal at both ends.

questions.question: Which problem is a natural queue application?
options: Hash function computation.
Binary search on a sorted array.
Breadth-first traversal.
Inorder traversal without any ordering requirement.
questions.explanation: Breadth-first traversal.

questions.question: Which structure is ideal for next-greater-element style problems?
options: A B-tree.
A binary heap only.
A monotonic stack.
A simple FIFO queue only.
questions.explanation: A monotonic stack.

questions.question: What does a monotonic deque maintain for a sliding-window maximum?
options: Only the minimum index ever seen.
Every element duplicated twice.
All elements in arbitrary order.
Candidate indices in decreasing value order while removing expired indices.
questions.explanation: Candidate indices in decreasing value order while removing expired indices.

questions.question: Which edge case is crucial in circular queues?
options: Distinguishing empty from full states.
Keeping every slot non-zero.
Using recursion for every operation.
Keeping the array sorted.
questions.explanation: Distinguishing empty from full states.

questions.question: What is the most common stack implementation bug with linked nodes?
options: Using a fixed matrix.
Failing to sort values.
Using a queue front instead of a stack top by definition.
Updating the top reference inconsistently during push/pop.
questions.explanation: Updating the top reference inconsistently during push/pop.

questions.question: What is the typical complexity of a single pass through an expression using a stack?
options: O(n^2) always.
O(1) for arbitrary n.
O(log n).
O(n).
questions.explanation: O(n).

questions.question: Why does Basic Calculator-style parsing need explicit handling of parentheses/sign state?
options: All operators have the same precedence and no nesting exists.
A queue cannot store numbers.
The evaluation order is not determined solely by left-to-right token processing.
Stacks cannot store characters.
questions.explanation: The evaluation order is not determined solely by left-to-right token processing.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem directly reinforces the two-stack queue simulation idea?
options: LeetCode #1584 — Min Cost to Connect All Points.
LeetCode #232 — Implement Queue using Stacks.
LeetCode #704 — Binary Search.
LeetCode #98 — Validate Binary Search Tree.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #232 — Implement Queue using Stacks.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem directly reinforces constant-time minimum retrieval from a stack?
options: LeetCode #912 — Sort an Array.
LeetCode #200 — Number of Islands.
LeetCode #704 — Binary Search.
LeetCode #155 — Min Stack.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #155 — Min Stack.

questions.question: What should a learner prove before declaring an expression evaluator complete?
options: Only that one sample matches.
Operand order, precedence/associativity, malformed input behavior, and complexity.
Only that the code uses a stack.
Only that the input is non-empty.

questions.question: Which data structure most naturally models browser backtracking through previously visited pages?
options: A stack representing the history of pending return states.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Master preorder, inorder, postorder, level-order, iterative stacks, and traversal properties.

### Invariant / contract
Every node is visited exactly once in a correct traversal.

### Complexity
O(n) time; O(h) recursion/stack for DFS; O(w) for BFS.

### Why it matters
Traversal order becomes a language for expressing tree computations.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Master preorder, inorder, postorder, level-order, iterative stacks, and traversal properties.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; struct Node{int x;Node*l,*r;Node(int v):x(v),l(nullptr),r(nullptr){}}; void inorder(Node*n){if(!n)return;inorder(n->l);cout<<n->x<<" ";inorder(n->r);} int main(){Node*r=new Node(2);r->l=new Node(1);r->r=new Node(3);inorder(r);}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Tree Traversals**?
options: Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Every node is visited exactly once in a correct traversal.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Tree Traversals is: Every node is visited exactly once in a correct traversal.

pages.content:
### When should you think about **Tree Traversals**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`tree/heap state: root 4 with children 2 and 6; then trace one insertion, rotation, traversal, or heap adjustment.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Tree Traversals.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){priority_queue<int,vector<int>,greater<int>>pq;for(int x:{9,2,7})pq.push(x);while(!pq.empty()){cout<<pq.top()<<" ";pq.pop();}}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Tree Traversals**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Every node is visited exactly once in a correct traversal.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
Only the final printed value.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Wrong visit order; enqueueing nulls unnecessarily.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Tree Traversals.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){priority_queue<int,vector<int>,greater<int>>pq;for(int x:{9,2,7})pq.push(x);while(!pq.empty()){cout<<pq.top()<<" ";pq.pop();}}

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Tree Traversals**?
options: Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Implement binary nodes, recursive size/height/leaf counts, and structural properties.

### Invariant / contract
Each node has at most two child links, and null links terminate branches.

### Complexity
Most structural computations O(n).

### Why it matters
Binary trees are the foundation for BSTs, heaps, and expression trees.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Implement binary nodes, recursive size/height/leaf counts, and structural properties.

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Binary Tree ADT**?
options: Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
Each node has at most two child links, and null links terminate branches.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Binary Tree ADT is: Each node has at most two child links, and null links terminate branches.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`tree/heap state: root 4 with children 2 and 6; then trace one insertion, rotation, traversal, or heap adjustment.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Binary Tree ADT.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){priority_queue<int,vector<int>,greater<int>>pq;for(int x:{9,2,7})pq.push(x);while(!pq.empty()){cout<<pq.top()<<" ";pq.pop();}}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Binary Tree ADT**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Only the final printed value.
Each node has at most two child links, and null links terminate branches.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Assuming completeness when none is given.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Build and evaluate trees representing arithmetic expressions and map traversals to prefix/infix/postfix forms.

### Invariant / contract
Each operator node combines the values of its child subexpressions.

### Complexity
Build/evaluate O(n).

### Why it matters
Expression trees separate syntax structure from execution.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Build and evaluate trees representing arithmetic expressions and map traversals to prefix/infix/postfix forms.

### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`tree/heap state: root 4 with children 2 and 6; then trace one insertion, rotation, traversal, or heap adjustment.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

### Core idea
Define ordering property and basic search, insert, minimum, maximum, predecessor, and successor operations.

### Invariant / contract
For each node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger under the chosen policy.

### Complexity
Average O(log n) in balanced cases; O(n) worst case.

### Why it matters
BSTs turn ordered search into a structural invariant.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;struct N{int x;N*l,*r;N(int v):x(v),l(nullptr),r(nullptr){}};N*del(N*n,int x){if(!n)return n;if(x<n->x)n->l=del(n->l,x);else if(x>n->x)n->r=del(n->r,x);else{if(!n->l){N*r=n->r;delete n;return r;}if(!n->r){N*l=n->l;delete n;return l;}N*s=n->r;while(s->l)s=s->l;n->x=s->x;n->r=del(n->r,s->x);}return n;}void in(N*n){if(!n)return;in(n->l);cout<<n->x<<" ";in(n->r);}int main(){N*r=nullptr;for(int x:{5,3,7,2,4,6,8}){if(!r)r=new N(x);else {N**p=&r;while(*p){if(x<(*p)->x)p=&(*p)->l;else p=&(*p)->r;}*p=new N(x);}}r=del(r,7);in(r);}

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;struct N{int x;N*l,*r;N(int v):x(v),l(nullptr),r(nullptr){}};long long rangeSum(N*n,int lo,int hi){if(!n)return 0;if(n->x<lo)return rangeSum(n->r,lo,hi);if(n->x>hi)return rangeSum(n->l,lo,hi);return n->x+rangeSum(n->l,lo,hi)+rangeSum(n->r,lo,hi);}int main(){N*r=new N(5);r->l=new N(3);r->r=new N(8);r->l->l=new N(2);r->l->r=new N(4);cout<<rangeSum(r,3,8);}

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; struct Node{int x,h;Node*l,*r;Node(int v):x(v),h(1),l(nullptr),r(nullptr){}}; int H(Node*n){return n?n->h:0;} int bal(Node*n){return n?H(n->l)-H(n->r):0;} Node*rotR(Node*y){Node*x=y->l;Node*t=x->r;x->r=y;y->l=t;y->h=max(H(y->l),H(y->r))+1;x->h=max(H(x->l),H(x->r))+1;return x;} int main(){Node*r=new Node(30);r->l=new Node(20);r->l->l=new Node(10);r=rotR(r);cout<<r->x;}

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Maintain height balance with LL, RR, LR, and RL rotations after updates.

### Invariant / contract
At every node, balance factor is -1, 0, or +1 after rebalancing.

### Complexity
Search/update O(log n); rotations O(1).

### Why it matters
AVL trees trade a little update work for strict height guarantees.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Maintain height balance with LL, RR, LR, and RL rotations after updates.

using namespace std; struct Node{int x,h;Node*l,*r;Node(int v):x(v),h(1),l(nullptr),r(nullptr){}}; int H(Node*n){return n?n->h:0;} int bal(Node*n){return n?H(n->l)-H(n->r):0;} Node*rotR(Node*y){Node*x=y->l;Node*t=x->r;x->r=y;y->l=t;y->h=max(H(y->l),H(y->r))+1;x->h=max(H(x->l),H(x->r))+1;return x;} int main(){Node*r=new Node(30);r->l=new Node(20);r->l->l=new Node(10);r=rotR(r);cout<<r->x;}

At every node, balance factor is -1, 0, or +1 after rebalancing.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for AVL Trees is: At every node, balance factor is -1, 0, or +1 after rebalancing.

**Not a fit when**

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`tree/heap state: root 4 with children 2 and 6; then trace one insertion, rotation, traversal, or heap adjustment.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Updating heights in wrong order, choosing wrong rotation.

pages.content:
### Core idea
Understand node coloring, root/leaf conventions, red-red violations, black-height, rotations, and fix-up ideas.

### Invariant / contract
No red node has a red child, and every root-to-leaf path has the same black height under the standard model.

### Complexity
Search/insert/delete O(log n).

### Why it matters
Red-black trees provide looser but efficient balancing used by standard libraries.

### Core idea
Implement array-indexed min/max heaps, sift-up, sift-down, heapify, and heapsort.

### Invariant / contract
Every parent satisfies the heap-order relation with its children.

### Complexity
Build-heap O(n); push/pop O(log n).

### Why it matters
Array layout removes explicit pointers while preserving tree structure.

using namespace std;void sift(vector<int>&a,int i,int n){while(true){int l=2*i+1,r=l+1,m=i;if(l<n&&a[l]>a[m])m=l;if(r<n&&a[r]>a[m])m=r;if(m==i)break;swap(a[i],a[m]);i=m;}}int main(){vector<int>a={3,1,6,5,2,4};for(int i=a.size()/2-1;i>=0;--i)sift(a,i,a.size());for(int x:a)cout<<x<<" ";}

pages.content:
### Core idea
Apply trees to hierarchical data, range/search problems, expression evaluation, priority scheduling, and interview patterns.

### Invariant / contract
The tree invariant should directly encode the application’s decision or aggregation rule.

### Complexity
Varies; often O(log n) with balanced ordered trees or O(n) traversal.

### Why it matters
Applications connect abstract tree properties to system-level decisions.

Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**

pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`tree/heap state: root 4 with children 2 and 6; then trace one insertion, rotation, traversal, or heap adjustment.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.

questions.question: Which property is part of a tree ADT’s basic structural definition?
options: All nodes must be stored contiguously in memory.
Every node must have exactly two children.
Every path may contain a cycle.
A root anchors the hierarchy and every node except the root has one parent in a tree.
questions.explanation: A root anchors the hierarchy and every node except the root has one parent in a tree.

questions.question: Which representation directly stores a binary node’s two child relationships?
options: A sorted array with no parent/child metadata.
A stack containing only the root value.
A hash table with one bucket for the entire tree.
A node record with left and right child references.
questions.explanation: A node record with left and right child references.

questions.question: Which traversal of a BST produces keys in sorted order under the usual strict BST invariant?
options: Preorder.
Inorder.
Level order.
Postorder.
questions.explanation: Inorder.

questions.question: What constraint defines the Binary Tree ADT?
options: The keys must be globally sorted.
Every node must have exactly one child.
Every level must contain the same number of nodes.
Each node has at most two children, conventionally called left and right.
questions.explanation: Each node has at most two children, conventionally called left and right.

questions.question: What is the recurrence intuition for binary-tree height?
options: Height is always O(1).
Height always equals the node count.
Height is unrelated to shape.
Height depends on the longest root-to-leaf path and grows with subtree height.
questions.explanation: Height depends on the longest root-to-leaf path and grows with subtree height.

questions.question: What does the BST invariant require?
options: The tree must be complete.
The root must be the minimum key.
Every node has exactly two children.
Keys in the left subtree are ordered below the node and keys in the right subtree above it, under the duplicate policy.
questions.explanation: Keys in the left subtree are ordered below the node and keys in the right subtree above it, under the duplicate policy.

questions.question: Why can an unbalanced BST degrade to O(n) search?
options: Inorder traversal stops working.
The tree can become a chain.
Binary search requires hashing.
The keys disappear.
questions.explanation: The tree can become a chain.

questions.question: Which BST deletion case is structurally hardest?
options: Deleting a leaf.
Deleting the root when it has no children.
Searching for a key.
Deleting a node with two children.
questions.explanation: Deleting a node with two children.

questions.question: What is the core AVL requirement?
options: All leaves are at identical depth.
Every node has two children.
The root is always the median of all keys.
The balance factor at each node remains within one in absolute value after rebalancing.
questions.explanation: The balance factor at each node remains within one in absolute value after rebalancing.

questions.question: Which AVL rotation fixes an LL-heavy subtree?
options: No rotation is ever needed.
A right rotation.
A double left rotation.
A left rotation.
questions.explanation: A right rotation.

questions.question: What distinguishes red-black trees from AVL trees in broad design terms?
options: Red-black trees cannot be searched.
Red-black trees store only integers.
Red-black trees use coloring and looser balance rules to guarantee logarithmic height.
AVL trees have no rotations.
questions.explanation: Red-black trees use coloring and looser balance rules to guarantee logarithmic height.

questions.question: What is the heap-order property of a min-heap?
options: Every parent key is less than or equal to its children.
Every child key is less than its parent.
The root is always the maximum.
The array is globally sorted.
questions.explanation: Every parent key is less than or equal to its children.

questions.question: What is the usual complexity of inserting into a binary heap?
options: O(n log n) for every insertion.
O(log n).
O(1) worst case.
O(n) always.
questions.explanation: O(log n).

questions.question: Why is bottom-up heap construction O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
options: Most nodes are near the leaves and require very little sift-down work.
The algorithm uses hashing.
Each node is inserted independently.
The heap is sorted first.
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near the leaves and require very little sift-down work.

questions.question: What does an expression tree represent?
options: A hash-table bucket layout.
A graph with arbitrary cycles.
The syntactic/operator structure of an expression.
Only the final numeric value.
questions.explanation: The syntactic/operator structure of an expression.

questions.question: Which application strongly matches a priority queue?
options: Repeatedly selecting the smallest/maximum pending item.
Maintaining a fixed parenthesis nesting state only.
Detecting string equality only.
Direct random access by array index.
questions.explanation: Repeatedly selecting the smallest/maximum pending item.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem reinforces inorder selection inside a BST?
options: LeetCode #704 — Binary Search.
LeetCode #230 — Kth Smallest Element in a BST.
LeetCode #912 — Sort an Array.
LeetCode #20 — Valid Parentheses.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #230 — Kth Smallest Element in a BST.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem best reinforces two-heap streaming median design?
options: LeetCode #295 — Find Median from Data Stream.
LeetCode #200 — Number of Islands.
LeetCode #155 — Min Stack.
LeetCode #34 — Find First and Last Position.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #295 — Find Median from Data Stream.

questions.question: What should be preserved after an AVL rotation?
options: Inorder key order and correct subtree heights.
The original pointer addresses.
Only the number of nodes.
Only the root value.
questions.explanation: Inorder key order and correct subtree heights.

questions.question: Which application is naturally modeled by a tree because the data is hierarchical?
options: A hash table keyed by student ID.
A file-system directory structure containing folders and files.
A stream of unrelated sensor readings with no parent-child relationship.
A flat list of daily temperatures with direct index access.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;struct N{vector<int>k;vector<N*>c;bool leaf;N(bool l):leaf(l){}};void splitChild(N*x,int i){N*y=x->c[i];N*z=new N(y->leaf);int mid=y->k.size()/2;int promote=y->k[mid];z->k.assign(y->k.begin()+mid+1,y->k.end());y->k.resize(mid);if(!y->leaf){z->c.assign(y->c.begin()+mid+1,y->c.end());y->c.resize(mid+1);}x->c.insert(x->c.begin()+i+1,z);x->k.insert(x->k.begin()+i,promote);}int main(){N*r=new N(false);N*y=new N(true);y->k={10,20,30};r->c.push_back(y);splitChild(r,0);cout<<r->k[0];}

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Distinguish internal separator nodes from leaf records, linked leaves, range scans, and update propagation.

### Invariant / contract
All records reside in linked leaves, and leaf links remain sorted.

### Complexity
Point/range queries O(log n + k) for k reported records.

### Why it matters
B+ trees are particularly effective for database-style range access.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Compare adjacency matrix, adjacency list, edge list, and compressed representations using workload trade-offs.

### Invariant / contract
Representation answers adjacency queries with known time/space trade-offs.

### Complexity
Matrix O(1) adjacency but O(V^2) space; list O(V+E) space.

### Why it matters
Representation choice can dominate practical performance.

callout.text: Compare adjacency matrix, adjacency list, edge list, and compressed representations using workload trade-offs.

Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
Representation answers adjacency queries with known time/space trade-offs.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Graph Representations is: Representation answers adjacency queries with known time/space trade-offs.

3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Traverse graphs level by level, compute unweighted shortest distances, and track visited state.

### Invariant / contract
When a node is first discovered in unweighted BFS, the recorded distance is minimal.

### Complexity
O(V+E) with adjacency lists.

### Why it matters
BFS converts graph distance in edges into queue levels.

topics.description: Master Topological Sort through concept construction, invariant-based reasoning, guided C++ implementation, independent practice, and LeetCode transfer where a direct problem mapping exists.

pages.title: Prerequisite Check
pages.content:
Before beginning **Topological Sort**, confirm the foundation: BFS/DFS, directed graphs.

**Ready check:** Explain the prerequisite in your own words and give one tiny example.

callout.title: Prerequisite takeaway

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){int n=4;vector<vector<int>>g={{1,2},{3},{3},{}};vector<int>in(n);for(auto&a:g)for(int v:a)in[v]++;queue<int>q;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(!in[i])q.push(i);while(!q.empty()){int u=q.front();q.pop();cout<<u<<" ";for(int v:g[u])if(--in[v]==0)q.push(v);}}

checkpoint.question: Which foundation should be checked before starting the topic **Topological Sort**?
options: Only memorising syntax without understanding the state model.
Skipping the prerequisite because all later operations are independent.

A completely unrelated algorithm with no dependency on this structure.
checkpoint.explanation: The prerequisite is BFS/DFS, directed graphs. and is needed to interpret the current topic correctly.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Order DAG vertices using indegrees (Kahn) or DFS finishing times; detect cycles.

### Invariant / contract
Every emitted vertex has no remaining unsatisfied incoming dependency.

### Complexity
O(V+E).

### Why it matters
Dependency scheduling is the canonical topological-sort application.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Order DAG vertices using indegrees (Kahn) or DFS finishing times; detect cycles.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){int n=4;vector<vector<int>>g={{1,2},{3},{3},{}};vector<int>in(n);for(auto&a:g)for(int v:a)in[v]++;queue<int>q;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(!in[i])q.push(i);while(!q.empty()){int u=q.front();q.pop();cout<<u<<" ";for(int v:g[u])if(--in[v]==0)q.push(v);}}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Topological Sort**?
options: The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
Every emitted vertex has no remaining unsatisfied incoming dependency.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Topological Sort is: Every emitted vertex has no remaining unsatisfied incoming dependency.

pages.content:
### When should you think about **Topological Sort**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`graph state: edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3; mark visited/discovery/low/dist/parent state after each step.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Topological Sort.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<vector<int>>g={{1,2},{0,3},{0,3},{1,2}};int edges=0;for(auto&v:g)edges+=v.size();cout<<edges/2;}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Topological Sort**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Only the final printed value.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
Every emitted vertex has no remaining unsatisfied incoming dependency.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Forgetting cycle detection; mixing edge direction.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Topological Sort.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<vector<int>>g={{1,2},{0,3},{0,3},{1,2}};int edges=0;for(auto&v:g)edges+=v.size();cout<<edges/2;}

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Topological Sort**?
options: Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Compute shortest paths from one source on non-negative weighted graphs using greedy finalization and a min-heap.

### Invariant / contract
When the minimum tentative distance is extracted, it is final under non-negative edge weights.

### Complexity
O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap and adjacency list.

### Why it matters
The relaxation invariant explains why Dijkstra works.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Compute shortest paths from one source on non-negative weighted graphs using greedy finalization and a min-heap.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`graph state: edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3; mark visited/discovery/low/dist/parent state after each step.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

codeCard.code:

Grow an MST outward from a chosen seed using the cheapest edge crossing the current cut.

### Invariant / contract
At every step the chosen edge is minimum across the cut separating selected and unselected vertices.

O(E log V) adjacency-list heap form.

Prim is a cut-property greedy algorithm.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Sort edges by weight and use DSU to accept edges that do not form a cycle.

### Invariant / contract
Accepted edges form a forest; each accepted edge joins two previously separate components.

### Complexity
O(E log E).

### Why it matters
Kruskal is edge-centric and works naturally with sparse edge lists.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Sort edges by weight and use DSU to accept edges that do not form a cycle.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Map routing, social connections, network reliability, dependency scheduling, recommender links, and resource networks to graph algorithms.

### Invariant / contract
The model must preserve the real system’s direction, weight, capacity, and update assumptions.

### Complexity
Varies with chosen algorithm and update rate.

### Why it matters
This topic integrates algorithms with engineering requirements.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Map routing, social connections, network reliability, dependency scheduling, recommender links, and resource networks to graph algorithms.

options: The model must preserve the real system’s direction, weight, capacity, and update assumptions.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Real-Time Applications of Graphs is: The model must preserve the real system’s direction, weight, capacity, and update assumptions.

pages.title: Pattern Recognition
pages.content:
### When should you think about **Real-Time Applications of Graphs**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`graph state: edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3; mark visited/discovery/low/dist/parent state after each step.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Real-Time Applications of Graphs.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<vector<int>>g={{1,2},{0,3},{0,3},{1,2}};int edges=0;for(auto&v:g)edges+=v.size();cout<<edges/2;}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Real-Time Applications of Graphs**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
Only the final printed value.
The model must preserve the real system’s direction, weight, capacity, and update assumptions.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Choosing algorithms without classifying the real-world graph.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Real-Time Applications of Graphs.

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Real-Time Applications of Graphs**?
options: Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

pages.title: Micro Practice
pages.content:
Try a tiny variation before opening a full solution. Change exactly one thing in the previous example: the empty case, a single element, a duplicate key, a boundary index, or one additional edge/node.

### Micro-practice
For **Real-Time Applications of Graphs**, change one condition from the dry run—such as an empty structure, a boundary position, a duplicate key, a disconnected vertex, a repeated value, or a different constraint. Predict the new state first, then implement only the changed step.

pages.content:
### Mastery checklist for **Real-Time Applications of Graphs**
- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.
- Identify when the pattern applies.

codeExamples.title: Real-Time Applications of Graphs — concept example
