#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>g={{{1,5},{2,2}},{{3,4}},{{3,7}}, {}};vector<int>d(4,1e9);d[0]=0;priority_queue<pair<int,int>,vector<pair<int,int>>,greater<pair<int,int>>>pq;pq.push({0,0});while(!pq.empty()){auto [du,u]=pq.top();pq.pop();if(du!=d[u])continue;for(auto [v,w]:g[u])if(d[v]>du+w)d[v]=du+w,pq.push({d[v],v});}cout<<d[3];}

questions.question: What makes a B-tree different from a binary search tree?
options: A B-tree has no ordering.
A B-tree stores multiple keys per node and can have many children.
A B-tree is always a graph cycle.
A B-tree stores one key total.

questions.question: Why are B-trees useful for external storage?
options: They eliminate sorting.
They store all records in one node.
High branching can reduce tree height and expensive block accesses.
They guarantee O(1) disk access.

questions.question: What is the key record-placement distinction in a B+ tree?
options: Leaves are unlinked.
Internal nodes contain no separators.
Actual records are stored in linked leaves while internal nodes guide search.
Records exist only in the root.
questions.explanation: Actual records are stored in linked leaves while internal nodes guide search.

questions.question: What is an adjacency list especially good for?
options: Sparse graphs where most possible edges are absent.
Only complete graphs.
Graphs with no vertices.
Constant-time access to every possible pair with low memory.
questions.explanation: Sparse graphs where most possible edges are absent.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of an adjacency matrix?
options: O(V^2) space in exchange for very fast direct adjacency checks.
It requires linked lists.
It cannot represent directed graphs.
It cannot represent weighted edges.
questions.explanation: O(V^2) space in exchange for very fast direct adjacency checks.

questions.question: Why must graph type be classified before algorithm selection?
options: Algorithm preconditions differ for direction, weights, cycles, and connectivity.
Every graph algorithm is identical.
Graph type affects only variable names.
Only traversal order matters.
questions.explanation: Algorithm preconditions differ for direction, weights, cycles, and connectivity.

questions.question: What invariant makes BFS shortest paths correct on unweighted graphs?
options: The graph must be a tree.
The queue remains sorted by vertex id.
The first discovery of a vertex occurs at the minimum number of edges from the source.
Every vertex is discovered twice.
questions.explanation: The first discovery of a vertex occurs at the minimum number of edges from the source.

questions.question: What is DFS commonly used for beyond traversal?
options: Binary search.
Hash-table resizing.
Cycle detection, components, and low-link structural analysis.
Constant-time sorting.
questions.explanation: Cycle detection, components, and low-link structural analysis.

questions.question: What does low[u] capture in articulation-point algorithms?
options: The number of children only.
The largest key in the subtree.
The BFS distance from the root.
The earliest discovery time reachable from the DFS subtree under the allowed back-edge rules.
questions.explanation: The earliest discovery time reachable from the DFS subtree under the allowed back-edge rules.

questions.question: What defines an Euler circuit?
options: A closed trail that uses every edge exactly once.
A shortest path between two vertices.
A tree with minimum weight.
A traversal that visits every vertex once regardless of edges.
questions.explanation: A closed trail that uses every edge exactly once.

questions.question: What is a key property of a topological ordering?
options: Every directed edge u→v places u before v.
Every vertex appears twice.
Edges are sorted by weight.
The graph must be undirected.
questions.explanation: Every directed edge u→v places u before v.

questions.question: When is Dijkstra’s algorithm valid in its standard form?
options: Edge weights are non-negative.
The graph must be unweighted only.
All weights are negative.
The graph must be a tree.
questions.explanation: Edge weights are non-negative.

questions.question: What does an MST optimize?
options: Number of vertices.
Maximum edge weight.
Shortest path from one chosen source to every vertex.
Total weight of a spanning tree connecting all vertices.
questions.explanation: Total weight of a spanning tree connecting all vertices.

questions.question: What is the greedy choice in Prim’s algorithm?
options: The globally largest edge.
The next vertex in numeric order.
The lightest edge crossing the cut between the built tree and the remaining vertices.
Any edge inside the built tree.
questions.explanation: The lightest edge crossing the cut between the built tree and the remaining vertices.

questions.question: What does DSU provide in Kruskal’s algorithm?
options: Topological order.
Efficient detection of whether an edge would connect two components or form a cycle.
Shortest paths.
Queue levels.
questions.explanation: Efficient detection of whether an edge would connect two components or form a cycle.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem reinforces Dijkstra on a weighted graph?
options: LeetCode #20 — Valid Parentheses.
LeetCode #704 — Binary Search.
LeetCode #912 — Sort an Array.
LeetCode #743 — Network Delay Time.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #743 — Network Delay Time.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem reinforces MST construction?
options: LeetCode #206 — Reverse Linked List.
LeetCode #155 — Min Stack.
LeetCode #1584 — Min Cost to Connect All Points.
LeetCode #34 — Find First and Last Position.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #1584 — Min Cost to Connect All Points.

questions.question: Which graph pattern models course prerequisites?
options: Directed acyclic dependency graph plus topological sort.
Circular queue only.
Hashing with open addressing.
Undirected MST only.
questions.explanation: Directed acyclic dependency graph plus topological sort.

questions.question: What must an Euler-trail implementation track carefully?
options: Only node colors.
Only visited vertices.
Consumed edges and the reconstruction order when backtracking.
Only shortest distances.
questions.explanation: Consumed edges and the reconstruction order when backtracking.

questions.question: Why does the real-time application step matter?
options: It forces the learner to model direction, weights, update frequency, and correctness requirements from real systems.
It makes all graph algorithms O(1).
It removes the need for complexity analysis.
It replaces graph modeling with code memorization.
questions.explanation: It forces the learner to model direction, weights, update frequency, and correctness requirements from real systems.

### Core idea
Define search as locating a key under an access model and choose algorithms using ordering, constraints, and query frequency.

### Invariant / contract
The search procedure maintains a set of candidates consistent with the observed information.

### Complexity
Depends on ordering and representation.

### Why it matters
Searching and preprocessing trade off upfront work against query speed.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Search sorted data by repeatedly discarding half the remaining candidate range.

### Invariant / contract
All candidates inside [l,r] remain possible and all outside have been eliminated.

### Complexity
O(log n) time, O(1) iterative space.

### Why it matters
Binary search is a boundary-invariant technique, not just a formula.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Search sorted data by repeatedly discarding half the remaining candidate range.

checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Binary Search is: All candidates inside [l,r] remain possible and all outside have been eliminated.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Build a sorted prefix by inserting each next value into its correct position.

### Invariant / contract
The prefix before the current index is always sorted.

### Complexity
O(n^2) worst; O(n) best for nearly sorted data; O(1) extra space.

### Why it matters
Excellent for small or nearly sorted inputs.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Build a sorted prefix by inserting each next value into its correct position.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<int>a={5,2,4,1};for(int i=1;i<(int)a.size();i++){int x=a[i],j=i-1;while(j>=0&&a[j]>x)a[j+1]=a[j--];a[j+1]=x;}for(int x:a)cout<<x<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Insertion Sort**?
options: All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
The prefix before the current index is always sorted.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Insertion Sort is: The prefix before the current index is always sorted.

pages.title: Pattern Recognition
pages.content:
### When should you think about **Insertion Sort**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`array/table state: [1, 3, 4, 7, 9] or slots [_, 10, _, 17, _]; trace the candidate range/shift/probe.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Insertion Sort.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){vector<int>a={7,3,5,1};sort(a.begin(),a.end());for(int x:a)cout<<x<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Insertion Sort**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Only the final printed value.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
The prefix before the current index is always sorted.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Moving the key before saving it.

callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Insertion Sort.

options: Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.

Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

using namespace std;long long inv(vector<int>&a,int l,int r){if(l>=r)return 0;int m=(l+r)/2;long long ans=inv(a,l,m)+inv(a,m+1,r);vector<int>b;int i=l,j=m+1;while(i<=m&&j<=r){if(a[i]<=a[j])b.push_back(a[i++]);else{ans+=m-i+1;b.push_back(a[j++]);}}while(i<=m)b.push_back(a[i++]);while(j<=r)b.push_back(a[j++]);copy(b.begin(),b.end(),a.begin()+l);return ans;}int main(){vector<int>a={2,4,1,3,5};cout<<inv(a,0,a.size()-1);}

pages.title: Prerequisite Check

checkpoint.question: Which foundation should be checked before starting the topic **Hashing Fundamentals**?

A completely unrelated algorithm with no dependency on this structure.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Understand hash tables, expected constant-time operations, load factor, and the relationship between key distribution and performance.

### Invariant / contract
A key maps deterministically to a bucket under a chosen hash function.

### Complexity
Expected O(1) search/insert/delete with good distribution; worst O(n).

### Why it matters
Hashing trades ordering for fast direct lookup.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Understand hash tables, expected constant-time operations, load factor, and the relationship between key distribution and performance.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;size_t h(int x,size_t m){return (unsigned)x%m;}int main(){for(int x:{10,22,31})cout<<h(x,7)<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Hashing Fundamentals**?
options: The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
A key maps deterministically to a bucket under a chosen hash function.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Hashing Fundamentals is: A key maps deterministically to a bucket under a chosen hash function.

pages.title: Pattern Recognition
pages.content:
### When should you think about **Hashing Fundamentals**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

callout.title: Recognition takeaway
callout.text: Understand hash tables, expected constant-time operations, load factor, and the relationship between key distribution and performance.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;size_t h(int x,size_t m){return (unsigned)x%m;}int main(){for(int x:{10,22,31})cout<<h(x,7)<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: Which signal is strongest evidence that a problem is a good fit for **Hashing Fundamentals**?
options: The problem title contains the word “data”.
The required operation and constraints match the structure’s strengths and invariant.
The input is large, so any data structure will automatically be optimal.
A solution is correct only when it uses recursion.
checkpoint.explanation: Pattern recognition comes from the operation/query requirements and constraints, not from keywords alone.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`array/table state: [1, 3, 4, 7, 9] or slots [_, 10, _, 17, _]; trace the candidate range/shift/probe.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Hashing Fundamentals.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){unordered_map<int,int>f;for(int x:{1,2,1,3})f[x]++;cout<<f[1];}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Hashing Fundamentals**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
A key maps deterministically to a bucket under a chosen hash function.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Only the final printed value.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Assuming hashes are unique, ignoring load factor.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Hashing Fundamentals.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;int main(){unordered_map<int,int>f;for(int x:{1,2,1,3})f[x]++;cout<<f[1];}

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Hashing Fundamentals**?
options: Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

pages.title: Micro Practice
pages.content:
Try a tiny variation before opening a full solution. Change exactly one thing in the previous example: the empty case, a single element, a duplicate key, a boundary index, or one additional edge/node.

### Micro-practice
For **Hashing Fundamentals**, change one condition from the dry run—such as an empty structure, a boundary position, a duplicate key, a disconnected vertex, a repeated value, or a different constraint. Predict the new state first, then implement only the changed step.

**Checkpoint:** state the invariant before running and state what changed after running.

callout.title: Micro Practice takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Hashing Fundamentals.

checkpoint.question: What should a micro-practice attempt for **Hashing Fundamentals** change first?
options: The problem statement and output contract.
The complexity requirement without changing the algorithm.
One controlled boundary or state variation while keeping the core invariant unchanged.
The entire algorithm and data representation simultaneously.
checkpoint.explanation: A micro practice should isolate one variation so the learner can transfer the concept instead of guessing.

pages.title: Independent Practice
pages.content:
Now solve the topic’s skill-builder and the mapped interview problems without copying the implementation. Start with the easiest problem, write the brute-force idea, then derive the Hashing Fundamentals solution.

**Before submit:** record the expected complexity, list three edge cases, and state one correctness invariant.

checkpoint.question: Before submitting an independent problem on **Hashing Fundamentals**, which combination is most important?
options: A correctness invariant, edge cases, and the expected time/space complexity.
Only the sample output.
Only the fastest-looking code, without proving correctness.
Only the number of lines of code.
checkpoint.explanation: Production-quality DSA practice combines correctness reasoning, edge-case coverage, and complexity analysis.

pages.title: Mastery Gate
pages.content:
### Mastery checklist for **Hashing Fundamentals**
- Explain the abstraction and why it exists.
- Identify when the pattern applies.
- Dry-run a fresh example.
- Implement the core operation without scaffolding.
- State correctness/invariant reasoning.
- State time and space complexity.
- Identify at least three edge cases.
- Solve one LeetCode transfer problem relevant to this topic.

**Common failure to avoid:** Assuming hashes are unique, ignoring load factor.

callout.title: Mastery takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Hashing Fundamentals.

checkpoint.question: Which outcome demonstrates mastery of **Hashing Fundamentals**?
options: Solve only the exact example seen in the lesson.
Recall the definition but cannot implement it.
Copy a memorized solution without tracing it.
Explain the pattern, implement it on an unseen case, justify correctness/complexity, and transfer it to interview practice.
checkpoint.explanation: Mastery requires explanation, implementation, reasoning, and transfer—not recall alone.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Design and evaluate hash functions for integers, strings, composite keys, and distribution quality.

### Invariant / contract
Equivalent keys must map consistently; unequal keys should spread broadly.

### Complexity
Hash computation ideally O(key length).

### Why it matters
Hash quality directly affects collision frequency.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Design and evaluate hash functions for integers, strings, composite keys, and distribution quality.

codeCard.code:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;size_t h(int x,size_t m){return (unsigned)x%m;}int main(){for(int x:{10,22,31})cout<<h(x,7)<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: Which statement most accurately captures the core rule of **Hash Functions**?
options: All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Equivalent keys must map consistently; unequal keys should spread broadly.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Hash Functions is: Equivalent keys must map consistently; unequal keys should spread broadly.

2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

Store colliding entries in per-bucket chains and analyze expected cost under load factor.

### Invariant / contract
Every key remains reachable from the bucket determined by its hash.

### Complexity
Expected O(1 + alpha) with alpha = n/m.

### Why it matters
Chaining tolerates high load factors but incurs pointer overhead.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Use probing sequences such as linear/quadratic probing and double hashing to keep entries in the table itself.

### Invariant / contract
Every occupied slot follows the table’s probe invariant for its key.

### Complexity
Expected O(1) at healthy load factors; performance degrades as table fills.

### Why it matters
Open addressing favors locality but needs careful deletion markers.

callout.title: Concept takeaway
callout.text: Use probing sequences such as linear/quadratic probing and double hashing to keep entries in the table itself.

The structure can violate its representation invariant as long as the final output looks plausible.
Implementation details are more important than the abstract contract.
All operations must be O(1), regardless of representation.
checkpoint.explanation: The defining invariant for Open Addressing is: Every occupied slot follows the table’s probe invariant for its key.

Understand directory depth, bucket local depth, splitting, and directory doubling for dynamic disk-oriented hashing.

### Invariant / contract
Directory prefixes identify buckets; local depth determines when a bucket must split.

### Complexity
Expected near O(1) bucket access with dynamic growth.

### Why it matters
Extendible hashing adapts bucket structure without rebuilding the entire file.

pages.title: Concept Build
pages.content:
### Core idea
Choose among search, sort, and hash strategies for interview and systems problems; compare preprocessing vs query cost.

### Invariant / contract
The algorithm should satisfy correctness and the required time/space constraints under the workload.

### Complexity
Varies by workload; common choices are O(log n), O(n log n), and expected O(1).

### Why it matters
This integration topic turns isolated techniques into algorithm-selection skill.

pages.content:
### When should you think about **Searching, Sorting and Hashing — Integrated Patterns**?
Look for problems where the representation or operation matches the lesson’s central invariant.

**Recognition signals**
- The problem statement naturally exposes the state described by the topic.
- The required operation should become simpler if the topic’s abstraction is used.
- Constraints reward the stated complexity profile.

**Not a fit when**
- The data access pattern contradicts the structure’s strengths.
- A simpler representation already satisfies the complexity requirement.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content:
### Guided dry run

Start with this deliberately small state:

`array/table state: [1, 3, 4, 7, 9] or slots [_, 10, _, 17, _]; trace the candidate range/shift/probe.`

Trace **one transition at a time**:
1. Record the initial state and the meaning of every pointer/index/reference.
2. Apply exactly one operation.
3. Re-check the topic invariant.
4. Continue until the requested result is reached.
5. Repeat once with a boundary case (empty/singleton/full/duplicate/disconnected/maximum-depth, as applicable).

**Do not code yet.** The purpose of this step is to make the state transition predictable before implementation.

callout.title: Dry Run takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Searching, Sorting and Hashing — Integrated Patterns.

codeCard.code:

using namespace std;int main(){vector<int>a={7,3,5,1};sort(a.begin(),a.end());for(int x:a)cout<<x<<" ";}

checkpoint.question: During a dry run of **Searching, Sorting and Hashing — Integrated Patterns**, what should be checked after each state transition?
options: Only the final printed value.
The algorithm should satisfy correctness and the required time/space constraints under the workload.
Whether the implementation uses the maximum possible memory.
Whether every line of code is executed exactly once.
checkpoint.explanation: Rechecking the invariant after transitions is the most reliable way to catch structural bugs early.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content:
### Build in small steps
1. Name the state variables and their meanings.
2. Initialize the representation in a valid base state.
3. Implement the smallest legal operation first.
4. Add the general case while preserving the invariant.
5. Handle the boundary cases explicitly.
6. Measure time and auxiliary space before optimizing further.

**Implementation warning:** Optimizing the wrong operation, missing worst-case behavior.

callout.title: Guided Build takeaway
callout.text: Continue only after you can explain the step for Searching, Sorting and Hashing — Integrated Patterns.

checkpoint.question: Which implementation practice is most important when building **Searching, Sorting and Hashing — Integrated Patterns**?
options: Modify multiple pointers/indices at once without recording their old values.
Choose an asymptotically slower method because the invariant is optional.
Update state in small steps while preserving the representation invariant and then handle boundaries.
Ignore boundary cases until production deployment.
checkpoint.explanation: Small, invariant-preserving updates make pointer/index-heavy algorithms easier to reason about and debug.

pages.content:

What edge cases challenge the representation?
What are the time and auxiliary-space costs?

masteryGate.commonFailure: Optimizing the wrong operation, missing worst-case behavior.

msa.title: Module 5 Assessment: SEARCHING, SORTING AND HASHING TECHNIQUES

questions.question: When is linear search a sensible choice?
options: The key space is always a hash table.
Every query requires O(log n) exactly.
The data is guaranteed sorted and huge.
The data is small, unsorted, or changes frequently enough that preprocessing is not worthwhile.
questions.explanation: The data is small, unsorted, or changes frequently enough that preprocessing is not worthwhile.

questions.question: What precondition does ordinary binary search require?
options: The array is a linked list.
Every value must be unique in all variants.
The current search range is ordered according to the comparison rule.
All values are negative.
questions.explanation: The current search range is ordered according to the comparison rule.

questions.question: What invariant is central to binary search?
options: The target, if present, remains inside the current candidate interval.
The left pointer only increases by one.
The midpoint is always the target.
The entire array is re-sorted each iteration.
questions.explanation: The target, if present, remains inside the current candidate interval.

questions.question: Why is insertion sort often good on nearly sorted data?
options: Its inner shifts can be small when each element is close to its final position.
It requires O(n) extra arrays.
It always runs in O(log n).
It does not use comparisons.
questions.explanation: Its inner shifts can be small when each element is close to its final position.

questions.question: What is Shell sort trying to improve?
options: Replace hashing.
Guarantee stability for every gap sequence.
Make every comparison O(1) regardless of memory.
Move far-apart inversions earlier so later insertion-style passes do less work.
questions.explanation: Move far-apart inversions earlier so later insertion-style passes do less work.

questions.question: What is the main idea of merge sort?
options: Repeatedly choose the global minimum with a heap only.
Insert each element into a BST.
Use hashing to eliminate all comparisons.
Recursively sort smaller halves and merge two sorted runs.
questions.explanation: Recursively sort smaller halves and merge two sorted runs.

questions.question: What does a good hash function aim to provide?
options: A unique bucket for every possible key.
Sorted keys by value.
Consistent mapping with broad distribution across buckets.
Guaranteed collision-free output.
questions.explanation: Consistent mapping with broad distribution across buckets.

questions.question: What does load factor alpha usually mean in a hash table?
options: Number of collisions divided by key length.
Number of stored entries divided by number of buckets/slots under the chosen model.
Number of probes in one operation.
Table size divided by number of keys squared.
questions.explanation: Number of stored entries divided by number of buckets/slots under the chosen model.

questions.question: Why does separate chaining handle collisions?
options: The keys are sorted globally.
The table rejects all collisions.
Every key is moved to a tree root.
Multiple colliding keys are stored in a per-bucket chain/container.
questions.explanation: Multiple colliding keys are stored in a per-bucket chain/container.

questions.question: What is a common deletion hazard in open addressing?
options: Deleting sorts the table.
Clearing a slot completely can break later probe sequences, so tombstones or reinsertion rules are needed.
Open addressing cannot delete.
Deletion makes all future hashes identical.
questions.explanation: Clearing a slot completely can break later probe sequences, so tombstones or reinsertion rules are needed.

questions.question: Why is rehashing required?
options: To make keys sorted.
To restore a healthy load factor and rebuild placements under the new capacity.
To remove all keys permanently.
To convert every table into a tree.
questions.explanation: To restore a healthy load factor and rebuild placements under the new capacity.

questions.question: What is distinctive about extendible hashing?
options: It requires the entire table to be rebuilt after every insertion.
A directory of prefixes and buckets with local/global depth supports dynamic splitting.
It never resizes.
It uses only one bucket.
questions.explanation: A directory of prefixes and buckets with local/global depth supports dynamic splitting.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem directly reinforces hash-map complement lookup?
options: LeetCode #102 — Binary Tree Level Order Traversal.
LeetCode #743 — Network Delay Time.
LeetCode #1 — Two Sum.
LeetCode #232 — Implement Queue using Stacks.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #1 — Two Sum.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem directly reinforces boundary-style binary search?
options: LeetCode #155 — Min Stack.
LeetCode #206 — Reverse Linked List.
LeetCode #34 — Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array.
LeetCode #200 — Number of Islands.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #34 — Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array.

questions.question: Which LeetCode problem reinforces binary search on an answer?
options: LeetCode #912 — Sort an Array.
LeetCode #147 — Insertion Sort List.
LeetCode #705 — Design HashSet.
LeetCode #875 — Koko Eating Bananas.
questions.explanation: LeetCode #875 — Koko Eating Bananas.

questions.question: Which sorting property is a classic strength of merge sort?
options: Stable O(n log n) sorting.
No recursion or iteration.
O(n) worst-case time without restrictions.
In-place O(1) auxiliary memory for the usual array implementation.
questions.explanation: Stable O(n log n) sorting.

questions.question: What is the primary reason hash tables can offer expected O(1) lookup?
options: Every key is stored twice.
The hash directs the key to a small expected set of candidate locations.
The table uses binary search on every key.
All keys are kept sorted.
questions.explanation: The hash directs the key to a small expected set of candidate locations.

questions.question: Why can binary search fail even when the code looks correct?
options: The data may not satisfy the ordering or boundary invariant the implementation assumes.
The language does not allow loops.
The array must contain only prime numbers.
The midpoint must always equal the target.
questions.explanation: The data may not satisfy the ordering or boundary invariant the implementation assumes.

questions.question: What should a final algorithm-selection decision compare?
options: Correctness preconditions, expected workload, worst/average complexity, memory, and implementation risk.
Only the input size, ignoring operations.
Only the number of lines of code.
Only whether a library call exists.
questions.explanation: Correctness preconditions, expected workload, worst/average complexity, memory, and implementation risk.

questions.question: Which integrated workflow best represents mastery of search/sort/hash?
options: Memorize one algorithm and reuse it everywhere.
Model → derive baseline → identify repeated work → choose representation → prove invariant → analyze complexity → test boundaries.
Ignore complexity until after deployment.
Start with the hardest code before understanding constraints.
questions.explanation: Model → derive baseline → identify repeated work → choose representation → prove invariant → analyze complexity → test boundaries.

learningObjectives: Select linear or binary search from ordering, query frequency, constraints, and access model.
Implement insertion, Shell, and merge sort and compare their invariants, stability, and complexity.
Explain hashing, collisions, load factor, and the relationship between hash quality and expected lookup time.
Implement separate chaining and open addressing and reason about probing and deletion markers.
Explain resizing/rehashing and extendible hashing using global/local depth and directory splits.
Combine searching, sorting, and hashing patterns in interview-style problems and justify complexity.

learningArchitecture.philosophy: Learners should never be expected to jump directly from a definition to a difficult problem. Each concept moves through understanding, intuition, tracing, guided implementation, independent practice, and mastery.

learnerJourney.name: Prerequisite Check
learnerJourney.purpose: Recall only the ideas required for the current topic.

learnerJourney.name: Concept Build
learnerJourney.purpose: Understand the data structure/algorithm and why it exists.

learnerJourney.name: Recognition
learnerJourney.purpose: Learn the signals that tell you when this technique applies.

learnerJourney.name: Visualize & Dry Run
learnerJourney.purpose: Trace a tiny example before writing code.

learnerJourney.name: Guided Implementation
learnerJourney.purpose: Build the solution in small, testable steps.

learnerJourney.name: Micro Practice

learnerJourney.name: Independent Practice
learnerJourney.purpose: Solve the topic practice set in increasing difficulty.

problemSolvingLoop: Choose the optimized data structure or algorithm
Dry run on normal + boundary cases
Reflect on why the solution works
learningArchitecture.masteryPolicy: Learners advance after they can explain the invariant, solve a fresh small variation, and justify complexity—not merely after reading a page.

learningPathNotes.route: Follow recommendedLearningOrder for the most gradual progression. Practice modules are intentionally placed after the concept modules they reinforce.
importantTransitions: ADT contracts → concrete representation → invariant-preserving operations → applications
BFS/DFS → structural graph analysis → shortest paths → MSTs → real-time network reasoning
Linear search → binary search → insertion/shell/merge sort → hashing and collision resolution
